newsitem.title: TURKEY: US pushes Kurd groups on truce, fighting reported.
newsitem.headline: US pushes Kurd groups on truce, fighting reported.

text.p: U.S. peace envoy Robert Pelletreau on Wednesday urged warring Iraqi factions to implement a ceasefire to end two months of fighting that has undercut Washington's anti-Baghdad policy.

"We have agreed on the desirability of ending the fighting...Turkey, the United States and the United Kingdom now call on both sides to implement this ceasefire in place beginning immediately," Pelletreau said in a statement.

Pelletreau said that in two days of talks in Turkey he had reached agreement in principle with Massoud Barzani, leader of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and Jalal Talabani of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) on a U.S.-sponsored truce.
Further meetings with delegations from each group were planned in Ankara next week with representatives of the U.S., Britain and Turkey. Pelletreau left Turkey on Wednesday.
"Each side will take defensive positions and not initiate firing or hostilities," said Pelletreau, U.S. assistant undersecretary of state for near eastern affairs.
But there were reports of skirmishes in the region hours after Pelletreau concluded his meetings late on Tuesday.
"The PUK started fighting just two hours after the talks," KDP Ankara representative Faik Nerweyi told Reuters. "There was a very huge attack on the Ranya area with the help of Iran."
The PUK, which denies any help from Tehran, said it had gone on the defensive and was not breaking the ceasefire.

United Nations officials in north Iraq on Wednesday negotiated a temporary truce between the city of Sulaimaniya -- which the PUK captured back from the KDP this month after losing it in September -- and Koy Sanjak for an aid convoy.

The sporadic fighting between the rival factions worsened on August 31 when Baghdad sent in tanks and troops to help Barzani take the main northern Iraqi city of Arbil, which had been in PUK hands for almost two years.
Numerous ceasefires between the two groups have been announced and broken since fighting first flared up in late 1994.

The two factions have been unable to agree on the distribution of toll money from the KDP-held Habur crossing into Turkey and the status of Arbil, the one-time seat of a joint parliament set up after the 1991 Gulf War.

Baghdad's involvement was met by U.S. cruise missile attacks on south Iraq, but despite an apparent respite brokered then by Pelletreau, the fighting continued although there was no sign that Iraqi troops were involved in the later clashes.

Washington, which leads an air operation set up after the Gulf War to protect the Kurds from Baghdad's troops, was forced to cancel aid, military and intelligence operations in the region when Barzani called on Iraq for help.
